n: Asaph cried out to God aloud, and God listened. The psalm then explains the long night that led to this point.
In trouble he sought the Lord; all night his hands were stretched out in prayer, and nothing could comfort him.

f.w: my sore ran in the night
f.g: Literally “my hand was stretched out in the night” — continual prayer.

f.w: my soul refused to be comforted

n: Strangely, thinking of God made him groan; his meditation only left him faint. Sometimes faith feels like a struggle before it brings peace.
God kept him from sleeping, and he was too upset even to talk.
He thought about the past — the old days, years long gone.
He remembered the songs he once sang at night, and searched his own heart for answers.
Then come six painful questions. First: has the Lord rejected us forever? Will he never again show favor?
Has his loyal love vanished? Has his promise failed for all time?
Has God forgotten how to be gracious? Has anger shut off his compassion? The questions themselves imply the answer — no, he hasn’t.

f.w: Hath God forgotten to be gracious?

n: The turning point: “This is my weakness” — or, “this is my grief.” Then he chooses to remember the years when God’s right hand acted for his people.

f.g: This is my sickness — or, “my grief is that God’s right hand has changed.” The Hebrew can be read both ways.

n: He resolves to remember God’s deeds and ancient wonders. Memory becomes medicine for despair.

f.w: I will remember the works of the LORD

n: He will meditate on all God has done and talk about it.
God’s way is holy. No god is as great as ours.
God works wonders and has shown his power among the nations.
With his strong arm he redeemed the descendants of Jacob and Joseph — all Israel — from Egypt.

f.w: the sons of Jacob and Joseph
f.g: Joseph is mentioned because his sons Ephraim and Manasseh became major tribes.

f.w: Thou hast with thine arm redeemed thy people

n: Now the Red Sea crossing is retold: the waters saw God and writhed in fear; the depths shook.
Clouds poured rain, thunder rolled, and lightning arrows flashed.
Thunder rumbled in the whirlwind, lightning lit the world, and the earth trembled.
God’s path went straight through the sea, yet no one could see his footprints. He was at work even when unseen — a comfort for anyone who feels God is absent.

f.g: His footprints were unseen, though he was truly present.

n: The psalm ends quietly: God led his people like a flock through Moses and Aaron. The great God of storms is also a gentle shepherd who works through his servants.

f.w: by the hand of Moses and Aaron
